deep.reconstruction:
Title: 'Quadratorum numeris primis divisorum residua lateralia', roughly 'residues of squares divided by prime numbers', i.e. quadratic residues for prime moduli. The archival mark is 40.c/1, and this is sheet (1) of a series; the next page continues the columns 97 to 223.

Layout. Rows give prime moduli p = 3, 5, 7, ..., 181, grouped in blocks of seven. Columns give primes q = 2, 3, 5, ..., 89. There are no numerals in the body. A small circle at (p, q) marks that q is a quadratic residue mod p, i.e. there is an x with x^2 ≡ q (mod p). In modern terms the circle means legendre_symbol(q, p) = +1. The diagonal cell q = p is also circled (q ≡ 0, trivially a 'residue').

Verification of this reading (my checks against the image):
- Row 3 has circles at q = 7, 13, 19, 31, 37, 43, 61, 67, 73, 79. These are exactly the q ≡ 1 (mod 3), plus the diagonal.
- Row 5 has circles at 11, 19, 29, 31, 41, 59, 61, 71, 79, 89. These are exactly the q ≡ ±1 (mod 5).
- Row 7 has circles at 2, 11, 23, 29, 37, 43, 53, 67, 71, 79. These are exactly the q ≡ 1, 2, 4 (mod 7).
- Row 13 has circles at 3, 17, 23, 29, 43, 53, 61, 79. These are the q ≡ 1, 3, 4, 9, 10, 12 (mod 13).
- Further spot checks: row 41 has 31 marked, and (31/41) = (-10/41) = +1. Rows 43, 79 and 83 also have 31 marked, which is correct.
- The reading is NOT 'p is a residue mod q'. Row 3 would then mark q ≡ ±1 (mod 12), which does not match the image.

Lines. Circles in horizontally or vertically adjacent cells are joined by segments, producing squares, chains and polyomino-like figures. This is a purely visual device for spotting patterns in the distribution of residues. It has no arithmetic content beyond adjacency.

Purpose (my interpretation). This is an empirical (inductive) table of Legendre symbols (q/p) for small primes. It is the kind of data from which the laws for which primes q are residues of which p (quadratic reciprocity) can be read off: compare the cell (p, q) with the cell (q, p) in the transposed position. It is evidently a working precursor of Tabula II of the Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), which lists for each prime modulus below 1000 which of -1 and the primes up to 97 are residues. It fits Gauss's own account of discovering reciprocity by induction in 1795.
errors: Possible omission (uncertain from image): row 11, column 31 appears unmarked, although 31 ≡ 9 = 3^2 (mod 11) is a residue.
Possible omission (uncertain from image): row 23, column 31 appears unmarked, although 31 ≡ 8 (mod 23) is a residue (2 is a residue mod 23 since 23 ≡ 7 mod 8).
Possible omission (uncertain from image): row 17, column 47 appears unmarked, although 47 ≡ 13 ≡ 8^2 (mod 17) is a residue. The column-47 chain seems to begin at row 19.
Otherwise every cell I spot-checked (rows 3, 5, 7, 13, 17, 19, 23 entirely; column 31 for rows 41-83) agrees with the Legendre symbol.

results.what: Table of quadratic residue character: for primes p ≤ 181 (rows) and q ≤ 89 (columns), circle iff q is a quadratic residue mod p
results.modern_name: Table of Legendre symbols (q/p); quadratic residue table
results.usually_credited_to: Such tables go back to Euler and Lagrange. The systematic prime-by-prime table is Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), Tabula II.

results.what: Empirical data underlying the inductive discovery of quadratic reciprocity (symmetry relation between (p/q) and (q/p))
results.usually_credited_to: Euler and Legendre (conjecture/statement); Gauss (inductive rediscovery 1795, first proof 1796)

results.what: Graphical joining of adjacent residue marks into figures to search for patterns
results.modern_name: Visual pattern search in a residue table (no modern theorem)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a computational table of quadratic residue characters. Such tables are well known to have been compiled by Gauss in his early number-theoretic period, and they culminated in Tabula II of the Disquisitiones. The connecting-line visualization is a curious personal device but carries no new mathematics.

checkable.asserts: Row 3 marks exactly these columns (q ≡ 1 mod 3).
The cells that appear unmarked in the image should be marked (possible slips).

checkable.sympy: all(legendre_symbol(p,q)*legendre_symbol(q,p)==(-1)**(((p-1)//2)*((q-1)//2)) for p in primerange(3,182) for q in primerange(3,90) if p!=q)
checkable.asserts: Quadratic reciprocity relates each cell (p,q) to its transposed cell (q,p) across this table.
Column 31 is correctly marked in rows 41, 43, 79, 83.

transcription_corrections: The interpretation should be explicit: a circle at (row p, column q) means q is a quadratic residue mod p, i.e. Legendre symbol (q/p) = +1, not the reverse.
Diagonal cells (p = q) are circled throughout (e.g. row 3/col 3, row 5/col 5, row 7/col 7, row 11/col 11).
The pencil note under the title reads 'Gauss Math 1.', with 'Gauss' faint/partly crossed. The archival number '40.c/1' is struck through and replaced by the circled '1'.
The red crayon stroke in the middle of the sheet (around rows 79-97, columns 31-41) is a later archival/library mark, not part of the table.
